title: Iroh 1.0 Distributed Systems Protocol: An APAC Build Guide
summary: How the Iroh 1.0 distributed systems protocol lets APAC teams build cross-border p2p apps with in-region relays, QUIC, and key-based dialling instead of US cloud.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** Iroh 1.0 is a Rust library that connects devices by cryptographic public key over QUIC, with stable wire protocol and API guarantees. For APAC teams it enables direct device-to-device paths plus self-hosted stateless relays in Singapore, Sydney or Tokyo — avoiding trans-Pacific round trips and cross-border transfer questions.


---


AWS publishes inter-region round-trip latency between its Asia Pacific (Singapore) and US East (N. Virginia) regions at well over 200 milliseconds — a physical floor set by the speed of light in fibre, not by anything an engineer can optimise away. Yet a startling number of apps built in Singapore, Taipei, Ho Chi Minh City and Sydney still route device-to-device traffic through us-east-1. The Iroh 1.0 distributed systems protocol is the clearest argument yet that they don't have to.


The core insight is simple and slightly uncomfortable: for a large class of product features — file sync, collaborative editing, device pairing, live cursors, local-first mobile apps, POS terminals talking to a back-office machine in the same shop — the cloud is not storage or compute. It's a relay. And a relay that lives 12,000 km away is an architectural choice, not a law of physics.

## What Iroh 1.0 actually commits to


Iroh is a Rust networking library from n0 that replaces IP addresses with cryptographic public keys as the primary addressing unit. You hold a 32-byte ed25519 public key for a peer, you call` connect()` , and the library's job is to find that peer and keep the connection alive regardless of whether it moved from Wi-Fi to 5G, changed NAT, or switched continents.


*Related reading:*[Salesforce Fin Acquisition: AI Agent Strategy for APAC Teams](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-fin-acquisition-ai-agent-strategy-apac)


The 1.0 release, announced on iroh.computer, makes two stability promises that matter far more than any feature:


- **Wire protocol stability.** A v1 endpoint will interoperate with other v1 endpoints. You can ship a mobile client today and not break it when you upgrade the server-side crate next quarter.
- **API stability.** The Rust API surface is frozen under semver for the 1.x line.


For anyone who has shipped on a pre-1.0 p2p stack, that's the whole story. The technical capability existed before; the ability to put it in a consumer app with a two-year support window did not.


Underneath, Iroh speaks QUIC directly — the IETF standardised QUIC as RFC 9000 in May 2021 — with TLS 1.3 for transport security. It does not invent a new crypto layer. That design decision has a knock-on consequence the heise.de coverage of the 1.0 release highlighted: because the encryption is end-to-end at the QUIC layer, Iroh's relay servers never terminate TLS and hold no per-connection session state. They forward opaque packets. Stateless relays are dramatically cheaper to run than stateful ones, which is exactly what makes the next section viable.


## Why NAT traversal is an Asia-Pacific problem specifically


Direct peer-to-peer connections fail when both sides sit behind NAT that won't cooperate. Iroh tries multiple paths simultaneously — LAN, IPv4 with hole punching, IPv6, relay — and promotes to the fastest one that works, falling back to relay when hole punching fails.


The hit rate matters commercially, because relay bandwidth is the line item you pay for. Tailscale, which pioneered much of the modern approach and documents it in detail in its "How NAT traversal works" engineering post, reports establishing direct connections in the large majority of attempts across its fleet, with the remainder falling back to its DERP relays. Iroh uses a comparable technique set.


Here's where the regional texture comes in. Mobile networks across Southeast Asia lean heavily on carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT) because of IPv4 scarcity, and CGNAT is the hardest case for hole punching. The counterweight is IPv6: APNIC's public IPv6 measurement data consistently shows India, Vietnam, Malaysia and Taiwan among the higher IPv6 deployment rates globally, with India frequently above 70% — materially ahead of several Western European markets. Where IPv6 is available end-to-end, NAT traversal is largely a non-problem.


*Related reading:*[Customer Data Platform ROI Measurement Framework for APAC Brands](https://branch8.com/posts/customer-data-platform-roi-measurement-framework)


So the practical APAC picture is bimodal. A Vietnamese consumer app on a Viettel 5G connection may get a clean IPv6 direct path. The same app on a hotel Wi-Fi network in Bangkok behind double NAT will need a relay. You need both, and you need the relay to be close.

## Running relays inside your own jurisdiction


This is the part most of the existing Iroh coverage underplays. Iroh ships with public relays operated by n0, which is fine for prototyping. For production in Asia-Pacific, you almost certainly want your own.


Two reasons, one technical and one legal.


Technically: a relay in Oregon serving two devices in Jakarta adds a trans-Pacific round trip to every packet on the fallback path. A relay in Singapore or Jakarta keeps that fallback within ~30–60 ms.


Legally: several APAC jurisdictions impose data localisation or transfer conditions that make "it transits a US server" a question your compliance team will ask. Vietnam's Decree 53/2022, implementing the Cybersecurity Law, sets out local storage and office requirements for defined categories of service providers. Indonesia's Government Regulation 71/2019 distinguishes public and private electronic system operators with different placement rules. India's DPDP Act 2023 empowers the government to restrict transfers to notified countries. China's PIPL sets cross-border transfer mechanisms administered by the CAC. None of these are automatically triggered by a stateless packet forwarder — but the argument is far easier when the forwarder is in-region and you control it.


Starting a relay is deliberately boring:


```text
1  cargo install iroh-relay    2  iroh-relay --config-path /etc/iroh/relay.toml
```


A minimal config, with TLS handled by Let's Encrypt:


```text
1  http_bind_addr = "0.0.0.0:80"    2  https_bind_addr = "0.0.0.0:443"    3
4  [tls]    5  hostname = "relay-sg.example.com"    6  cert_mode = "lets_encrypt"    7
8  [limits]    9  # cap per-client relay throughput so one peer can't    10  # eat the egress budget for the region    11  max_bytes_per_second = 1_000_000
```


Then point your endpoints at it rather than the defaults:


```text
1  use iroh::{Endpoint, RelayMode, RelayMap, RelayUrl};    2
3  let relays = RelayMap::from_iter([    4      RelayUrl::from("https://relay-sg.example.com".parse::<url::Url>()?),    5      RelayUrl::from("https://relay-syd.example.com".parse::<url::Url>()?),    6  ]);    7
8  let endpoint = Endpoint::builder()    9      .relay_mode(RelayMode::Custom(relays))    10      .discovery_n0()    11      .bind()    12      .await?;
```


Three relays — Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo — on small VMs will cover most of Asia-Pacific plus Oceania. Because the relays are stateless and don't decrypt anything, sizing is a bandwidth exercise, not a memory-per-session exercise. Check the exact option names against the current docs at docs.rs/iroh before you build; the snippets above are illustrative of shape, not copy-paste gospel.


## Dialing keys, not IPs: the minimum viable app


The programming model is small enough to read in one sitting, which is a large part of why` iroh p2p` discussions on the Rust subreddit and Hacker News have been broadly positive about ergonomics.


Accepting side:


```text
1  use iroh::{Endpoint, protocol::Router};    2
3  const ALPN: &[u8] = b"acme/sync/0";    4
5  #[tokio::main]    6  async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {    7      let endpoint = Endpoint::builder()    8          .discovery_n0()    9          .bind()    10          .await?;    11
12      println!("my node id: {}", endpoint.node_id());    13
14      let router = Router::builder(endpoint)    15          .accept(ALPN, SyncHandler::default())    16          .spawn();    17
18      tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await?;    19      router.shutdown().await?;    20      Ok(())    21  }
```


Dialing side:


```text
1  let conn = endpoint.connect(peer_node_id, ALPN).await?;    2  let (mut send, mut recv) = conn.open_bi().await?;    3  send.write_all(b"hello from sydney").await?;    4  send.finish()?;    5  let reply = recv.read_to_end(64 * 1024).await?;
```


Note what's absent: no IP, no port, no STUN server configuration, no signalling channel of your own. The ALPN string namespaces your protocol so multiple protocols can share one endpoint — useful when you want sync, file transfer and control messages over a single connection budget.


The practical implication for mobile teams: because the identity is a key and not an address, a phone that switches from office Wi-Fi to LTE in a lift keeps the logical connection. QUIC's connection migration plus Iroh's multipath probing handle the churn. Anyone who has written reconnection logic for a WebSocket on an Indonesian commuter train will recognise how much code that deletes.

## Iroh versus libp2p, Tailscale, and just using the cloud


Honest comparison, because the choice is genuinely contextual.


### Against libp2p


libp2p is the more complete toolkit: more transports, more DHT options, a mature pubsub layer, implementations in Go, Rust and JS. If you're building something blockchain-adjacent or need gossip across thousands of nodes, libp2p's surface area is a feature. Iroh is narrower by design — QUIC-only, key-based dialling, bring your own application protocol. Narrower means less to learn and less to break. For a product team shipping a feature rather than a network, that trade usually favours Iroh.


### Against Tailscale or a VPN mesh


Iroh is not a VPN, a point the n0 team has repeated in community threads. A VPN moves your whole machine onto an overlay network and is an infrastructure/IT product. Iroh is a library you link into one application. If you want your engineers to reach staging boxes, use a VPN. If you want your app to reach another instance of your app on a customer's phone, use Iroh.


### Against centralised cloud


The cloud wins on auditability, on anything requiring a single source of truth, and on features where both peers are rarely online simultaneously. It loses on latency for same-region device pairs, on egress cost at scale, and on the regulatory surface area of cross-border transfer. Most real systems end up hybrid: authoritative state in a regional database, hot path peer-to-peer.


## The trade-offs nobody puts in the launch post


**Rust-first.** Iroh is a Rust library. There are FFI paths and community bindings, and Swift/Kotlin integration via uniffi-style wrappers is practical, but your mobile team will be maintaining a cross-compilation pipeline. Budget for it.


**Offline peers.** Two devices that are never online at the same time cannot sync directly. You need a cloud-hosted always-on node in the mesh — which is fine, and cheap, because it's just another Iroh endpoint on a VM in your region, not a bespoke sync service.


**Observability regresses.** Centralised architectures give you one place to look. Mesh traffic doesn't hit your logs. Plan instrumentation before launch, not after the first support ticket.


**Key management is now your problem.** Node IDs are identity. Losing one is losing a device's identity; leaking one is a different class of incident than a leaked session token. Decide early how keys are provisioned, rotated and revoked.


**Enterprise networks.** Corporate firewalls that block UDP outright will force everything through relay over 443. It works, but you lose the latency win in exactly the environments where a B2B product lives.

## Staffing a Rust networking project across Asia-Pacific


I'll put my hiring hat on, because this is the question that actually kills these projects.


Rust systems engineers are the scarce resource. In the Stack Overflow Developer Survey, Rust has ranked as the most-admired language for several consecutive years, but admiration is not supply — the same surveys consistently put actual Rust usage in the low double digits of respondents. The gap between "wants to write Rust" and "has shipped async Rust networking in production" is wide.


Market by market, the shape differs. Vietnam and the Philippines have deep, fast-scaling pools for application and mobile engineering, but senior Rust systems specialists are thin on the ground and command a significant premium over the local Node or Java median. Taiwan and Singapore have stronger embedded and infrastructure backgrounds — Taiwan's hardware industry produces engineers genuinely comfortable with C/C++ memory models, which is the shortest path to productive Rust. Australia and New Zealand have the senior architects but at Western cost levels.


The structure that works, and the one I'd recommend from watching distributed teams across six-plus countries: one or two senior Rust engineers owning the networking crate, and a larger application team in Vietnam or the Philippines consuming a clean, documented internal API over FFI. Don't ask ten engineers to learn lifetimes. Ask two, and give the other eight a boundary they can work against.


A pattern we've seen from the managed-team side: a regional logistics software provider wanted driver devices to sync job state with a depot machine without a round trip to a US region, mostly for the dead-zone case rather than for privacy. The useful move wasn't the protocol choice at all. It was separating the transport crate from the business logic early enough that the app team never needed to touch Tokio. That boundary is the architectural decision; Iroh versus the alternative is downstream of it.


## Getting started without committing the roadmap


If you want to evaluate rather than adopt, the on-ramp is short.` cargo add iroh` plus the examples in the n0-computer/iroh GitHub repository will get two machines talking in under an hour. The iroh.computer docs carry a tutorial track, and the repository's` examples/` directory is the closest thing to the "Iroh 1.0 tutorial" people search for. Run it between a laptop in your office and a phone on mobile data — that single test tells you more about your users' NAT reality than any benchmark.


The broader direction of travel is worth naming. Cloudflare's Radar data shows HTTP/3 — and therefore QUIC — now carrying a substantial and growing share of global web traffic, which means the UDP path Iroh depends on is increasingly well-treated by middleboxes rather than dropped. Regulatory pressure on cross-border data flows in Asia is tightening, not loosening. Device compute keeps getting cheaper relative to cloud egress. Each of those trends independently makes direct connections more attractive, and the Iroh 1.0 distributed systems protocol is the first toolkit in this space with stability guarantees strong enough to bet a product roadmap on.


Before you commit, work through this checklist:


- **Are both peers typically online at the same time?** If no, you need an always-on node anyway — size that first.
- **Does same-region latency actually change the product?** If users can't feel 200 ms, the cloud is simpler.
- **What's your current egress bill for device-to-device traffic?** If it's immaterial, this is an engineering indulgence.
- **Do you have, or can you hire, two senior Rust engineers within your timeline?** Not ten. Two.
- **Which jurisdictions do your users sit in, and does a US-hosted relay create a transfer question?** Answer it with counsel, not with a blog post.
- **Can you run three relays — Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo — and monitor them?** If relay ops has no owner, it will rot.
- **Have you decided how node keys are provisioned and revoked?** Write it down before the first commit.
- **Is your mobile FFI pipeline resourced?** Cross-compilation is the most commonly underestimated item on this list.


If you answer yes to six or more, build the spike. If you answer yes to three, keep the cloud and revisit in two quarters.
